## Proof

**Claim:** Yes, there exists a function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ whose graph is dense in $\mathbb{R}^2$, i.e., every open disc in $\mathbb{R}^2$ contains a point of the graph.

### Key observation

The collection $\mathcal{B}$ of all open discs in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with rational center $(p,q)\in\mathbb{Q}^2$ and rational radius $r\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}$ is **countable** and forms a **basis** for the standard topology on $\mathbb{R}^2$. In particular, every open disc $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ contains some $B\in\mathcal{B}$.

Therefore, it suffices to construct $f$ so that its graph meets every disc in the countable family $\mathcal{B}$.

### Construction

Enumerate $\mathcal{B}=\{B_1, B_2, B_3, \dots\}$. We define $f$ on a countable set of distinct real numbers $\{x_1, x_2, \dots\}$ and set $f(x)=0$ elsewhere.

**Inductive step.** Suppose $x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}$ have been chosen (all distinct) and $f(x_i)$ defined for $i<n$. Consider $B_n$. Since $B_n$ is a nonempty open disc, it contains **uncountably many** points, hence points with uncountably many distinct $x$-coordinates. Only finitely many $x$-values $\{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}\}$ are forbidden. So we may pick

$$(x_n, y_n) \in B_n \quad\text{with}\quad x_n \notin \{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}\}.$$

Set $f(x_n)=y_n$.

After completing the induction, define $f(x)=0$ for all $x\notin\{x_1,x_2,\dots\}$. This gives a well-defined function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ (each real number is assigned exactly one value).

### Verification

Let $D$ be any open disc in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, there exists $B_n\subseteq D$ for some $n$. By construction, $(x_n, y_n)\in B_n\subseteq D$, and $(x_n,y_n)=(x_n,f(x_n))$ lies on the graph of $f$. Hence the graph of $f$ meets $D$.

If "disc" is interpreted as a **closed** disc, note that every closed disc of positive radius contains an open disc, so the same conclusion holds.

### Conclusion

The function $f$ constructed above has a graph that intersects every disc in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Therefore, such a function **exists**. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
